C005.subject: Raising the minimum wage in markets with strong employer monopsony power
C005.object: a reallocation of hours from low-skilled workers to higher-skilled part-time workers, increasing within-firm wage inequality
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Raising the minimum wage in markets with strong employer monopsony power a reallocation of hours from low-skilled workers to higher-skilled part-time workers, increasing within-firm wage inequality]

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal firm-level payroll data from countries with minimum wage increases (e.g., U.S. Census Bureau's Longitudinal Employer-Household Dynamics data) to track changes in hours allocation and wage inequality within firms across skill levels. — Directly tests the hypothesis by observing whether firms reallocate hours from low-skilled to higher-skilled part-time workers after a minimum wage hike, and whether within-firm wage inequality increases, using natural variation in policy implementation.

[PATH:theoretical] Labor market search-and-matching models incorporating monopsony power and heterogeneous worker skills, calibrated to low-skilled labor markets. — Provides a causal mechanism to examine whether a binding minimum wage in monopsonistic settings leads to hour reallocation and wage dispersion, allowing counterfactual simulations to isolate the effect from confounding factors.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of existing empirical studies on minimum wage effects in monopsonistic labor markets, focusing on within-firm hour allocation and wage inequality outcomes. — Synthesizes evidence from multiple contexts to assess the generalizability of the hypothesis, identifying conditions under which the predicted reallocation and inequality effects are observed or absent.

C006.subject: Raising the minimum wage in markets with strong employer monopsony power
C006.object: increased employment and improved conditions for low-skilled workers
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Raising the minimum wage in markets with strong employer monopsony power increased employment and improved conditions for low-skilled workers]

[PATH:empirical] Quasi-experimental studies of minimum wage increases in U.S. states with concentrated low-wage labor markets (e.g., county-level Herfindahl index for fast food or retail) — Directly tests the hypothesis by comparing employment and wage outcomes in high-monopsony vs. competitive local markets, leveraging policy variation since the 1990s.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of minimum wage employment effects with moderator variables for labor market concentration (e.g., Doucouliagos & Stanley, 2009; updated with recent data) — Synthesizes existing empirical evidence to assess whether monopsony power systematically alters the sign or magnitude of employment effects, providing a broader inferential base.

[PATH:theoretical] Structural labor market model calibrated to developed-country local labor markets with employer concentration (e.g., Manning, 2003; Berger et al., 2022) — Simulates counterfactual minimum wage changes under varying monopsony degrees, isolating causal mechanisms and identifying conditions under which employment increases.

qualifier.geographic: developed countries with localized labor markets

C007.subject: Raising the minimum wage in markets with strong employer monopsony power
C007.object: overall labor income for low-skilled workers due to offsetting reductions in hours and fringe benefits
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Raising the minimum wage in markets with strong employer monopsony power overall labor income for low-skilled workers due to offsetting reductions in hours and fringe benefits]

[PATH:empirical] Quasi-experimental studies of minimum wage increases in highly concentrated local labor markets (e.g., using county-level Herfindahl-Hirschman Index to proxy monopsony power) that track changes in hours, fringe benefits, and total earnings for low-skilled workers — Directly tests the hypothesis by examining whether firms in monopsonistic markets offset wage increases by reducing hours and benefits, leading to lower overall income.

[PATH:empirical] Firm-level survey or administrative data on non-wage compensation (e.g., health insurance, paid leave, schedule flexibility) before and after a minimum wage policy change, focusing on industries with few employers (e.g., rural retail, fast food) — Provides evidence on the specific offsetting mechanism (fringe benefit cuts) that the hypothesis depends on, which is often overlooked in aggregate studies.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical models of monopsony with endogenous fringe benefits and labor supply elasticity (e.g., extensions of the Manning (2003) dynamic monopsony framework) — Clarifies the conditions under which a minimum wage reduces total compensation, helping to refine the hypothesis and identify when the predicted effect is most likely to hold.

qualifier.condition: if firms respond to the wage floor by cutting non-wage compensation and adjusting work schedules to minimize total labor costs

C008.subject: Raising the minimum wage in markets with strong employer monopsony power
C008.object: overall labor income for low-skilled workers due to potential job losses and reduced hours
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Raising the minimum wage in markets with strong employer monopsony power overall labor income for low-skilled workers due to potential job losses and reduced hours]

[PATH:empirical] Quasi-experimental studies of minimum wage increases in U.S. counties with high employer concentration (e.g., using Herfindahl-Hirschman Index) during periods of weak labor demand, analyzing employment and hours changes for low-skilled workers via difference-in-differences or event study designs. — Directly tests the hypothesis by exploiting variation in monopsony power and labor market conditions, providing causal estimates of wage impacts on total labor income.

[PATH:theoretical] Structural labor market models incorporating monopsony power and labor demand elasticities, calibrated to U.S. low-skilled markets during low-inflation periods, simulating the effect of minimum wage hikes on employment, hours, and income distribution. — Allows for counterfactual analysis under controlled assumptions about monopsony strength and demand shocks, clarifying mechanisms and parameter sensitivity.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of empirical minimum wage studies focusing on low-skilled workers in concentrated labor markets, with subset analysis by labor demand conditions (e.g., recession vs. expansion) and inflation regimes. — Synthesizes existing evidence to assess whether job loss and reduced hours effects dominate income gains in the specified temporal and geographic scope, identifying gaps and consistency.

qualifier.temporal: during periods of weak labor demand and low inflation
qualifier.geographic: in low-skilled labor markets with strong employer monopsony power in the United States

C011.subject: Raising the minimum wage in markets with strong employer monopsony power
C011.object: the disemployment effect for low-skilled workers when combined with a targeted wage subsidy for thin-margin firms
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Raising the minimum wage in markets with strong employer monopsony power the disemployment effect for low-skilled workers when combined with a targeted wage subsidy for thin-margin firms]

[PATH:empirical] Quasi-experimental analysis of state-level minimum wage increases with concurrent small-business subsidy programs (e.g., Medicaid expansion or targeted tax credits) in retail and hospitality sectors, using ACS or CPS data to measure employment changes for low-skilled workers by firm profit margin. — Directly tests the combined policy effect in real-world settings where monopsony power and thin margins coexist, providing causal estimates of disemployment reduction.

[PATH:theoretical] Structural labor market model calibrated to monopsonistic retail/hospitality sectors, simulating minimum wage increases with and without a wage subsidy for firms with profit margins below 3%, using parameters from existing monopsony and firm heterogeneity literature. — Allows counterfactual analysis of the interaction effect, isolating the subsidy's role in offsetting disemployment when firms have wage-setting power and thin profit buffers.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of minimum wage studies that include firm-level profit margin or market concentration as moderators, combined with studies of wage subsidies (e.g., Earned Income Tax Credit or wage insurance) for small firms. — Synthesizes existing evidence on the separate effects and their potential interaction, identifying gaps and conditions under which the combined policy may reduce disemployment.

scope.domain: low-skilled labor markets with monopsony and thin profit margins

qualifier.policy_interaction: wage subsidy for firms with profit margins below 3%

C012.subject: Raising the minimum wage in markets with strong employer monopsony power

evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Raising the minimum wage in markets with strong employer monopsony power increased employment and reduced turnover for low-skilled workers in industries with thin profit margins]

[PATH:empirical] Quasi-experimental studies comparing employment and turnover in U.S. states with high employer concentration (e.g., Herfindahl-Hirschman Index above 2500) that implemented minimum wage increases during low-demand periods, using synthetic control methods or difference-in-differences. — Directly tests the causal claim by isolating monopsony conditions and thin-margin industries, controlling for aggregate demand and inflation.

[PATH:empirical] Firm-level administrative data from thin-margin service industries (e.g., fast food, retail) in high-concentration local labor markets, analyzing wage, employment, and turnover changes after minimum wage hikes. — Provides granular evidence on employer responses and worker outcomes, capturing turnover dynamics and profit margin constraints.

[PATH:literature] Re-analysis of existing meta-studies on minimum wage employment effects, focusing on studies that explicitly measure employer market power (e.g., labor supply elasticity to the firm) and profit margins. — Synthesizes prior evidence to assess whether the hypothesized effects hold across different monopsony and margin contexts, identifying gaps or conflicting results.

scope.domain: low-skilled labor markets with monopsony and thin profit margins

qualifier.temporal: during periods of low aggregate demand and stable inflation
qualifier.geographic: in U.S. states with high employer concentration and thin-margin service industries
